app.title: Orrery — four models of the solar system
app.subtitle: Ptolemy · Copernicus · Kepler · Newton
mode.label: Model
engine.label: Variant
engine.help.ptolemaic-reframe: Accurate positions expressed with Earth at the centre. What Ptolemy was approximating.
engine.help.ptolemaic-epicyclic: Ptolemy's actual construction with Almagest parameters, errors included.
engine.help.circular: Every orbit a plain circle about the Sun, gone round uniformly. Not Copernicus's model — the simplification people mistake for it. Useful for one thing: seeing what the eccentric bought him, and how much of an orbit's shape the eccentricity alone accounts for.
engine.help.nbody: Numerical integration of Newton's law of gravity. Orbits are not prescribed. They emerge — as Kepler's ellipses, now a consequence rather than an assumption. The integration is a modern technique: Newton solved the two-body case in closed form and handled the rest by perturbation.

harness.label: What to show
harness.sightlineBend: The sight-line bends at the body. Compressed scale distorts every angle measured from anywhere but the centre of the map. The line runs through the body rather than straight past it, because a line that misses what it points at would be worse. At true scale the bend all but disappears. In Ptolemy's view, where Earth is also the centre, it goes entirely.
harness.trailsEmpty: Orbits are drawn from positions actually visited, not computed in advance. Run the clock and the trail builds.
harness.trailsRecorded: {{days}} days recorded, {{step}}-day steps. Longer history is kept more coarsely.
harness.hoverNote: Hover over any part of the construction — a circle, an arm, the equant, a force vector — to read what it is and what it measures right now.
harness.note.deferent.ptolemaic: The great circle — and it carries the centre of the epicycle, never the planet itself. Its own centre is displaced from {{centreOf}}, and that displacement is the eccentricity. The radius is 60 by definition: the Almagest fixes no absolute distance anywhere, so every other length in the model is stated against this one.
harness.note.deferent.ptolemaic.satellit: Ptolemy's eccentric, stretched to cover a moon the way his solar model would have had to be. {{bodyOf}} sits off the centre of its own circle, and the motion runs uniform about a second point further out. No epicycle here. In his planetary models the epicycle carries the Earth's own orbit, and a moon seen from its planet has no such term.
harness.note.deferent.copernican: Copernicus's eccentric circle, of the orbit's true semi-major axis. Its centre stands off {{centreOf}} by three halves of ae and the epicyclet riding on it carries the other half. That pair is his replacement for the equant, which he rejected because it makes a circle turn non-uniformly about its own centre.
harness.note.deferent.circle: One circle at the mean distance, centred on {{centreOf}} itself. That is the whole model. On these orbits it is a good one too — which is what makes the eccentrics and epicycles elsewhere look like answers to a real question rather than decoration.
harness.note.epicycle.ptolemaic: The small circle the planet actually rides. For an outer planet it carries the Earth's own annual motion in disguise — which is why it keeps step with the Sun, and why retrograde happens at opposition; for an inner planet it carries the planet's own year instead.
harness.note.epicycle.copernican: The epicyclet: a small circle of half ae, turning at twice the mean anomaly. With the eccentric it reproduces the equant to first order in e. Same accuracy, and every motion stays uniform about a real centre — which was Copernicus's whole objection.
harness.note.orbit.kepler: One ellipse, with {{centreOf}} at a focus and nothing at the centre. It replaces every circle before it: no deferent, no epicycle, no equant. Its shape is very nearly a circle, so what the eye actually sees is not the flattening but where {{centreOf}} sits.
harness.note.orbit.newton: The same conic, arrived at rather than fitted. A body pulled toward a fixed centre as 1/r² moves on a conic with that centre at a focus — Principia I, XI. So this figure is a result. Give the force and there is nothing left to describe.
harness.note.centre.ptolemaic: The centre of the deferent, and nothing whatever sits here. {{centreOf}} is off to one side, and the motion is not uniform about this point either: that is what the equant was invented to fix.
harness.note.centre.copernican: The centre of Copernicus's circle, displaced from {{centreOf}} by three halves of ae. Nothing sits here. The displacement is the eccentricity, split between this offset and the epicyclet.
harness.note.centre.kepler: The ellipse's geometric centre — the point that governed everything before Kepler and governs nothing after him. {{centreOf}} is not here; it is at the focus, a whole ae away.
harness.note.centre.circle: The centre of the circle, which is {{centreOf}} itself. Nothing is displaced in this model and nothing needs to be: one circle, gone round uniformly.
harness.note.focus.occupied: The focus the body really goes round — {{centreOf}} is here. That is the first law: not at the centre but at a focus, and the two stand a whole ae apart.
harness.note.focus.empty: The other focus. Nothing occupies it. It is drawn because it is empty. An ellipse has two foci, {{centreOf}} holds one, and the bare one is the sharpest evidence that this is no circle with its centre shifted.
harness.note.equant: Ptolemy's cleverest device. It is also invisible in the finished orbit. The arm sweeps equal angles in equal times about this point — not about the centre of the circle, and not about {{centreOf}}. That is what let a circle speed up and slow down the way a real orbit does. Copernicus threw it out. Kepler's ellipse is what finally replaced it.
harness.note.deferent-arm.ptolemaic: The arm carrying the epicycle's centre round the deferent. It starts at the equant, not at the centre, because the equant is the point the motion is uniform about. Its rate holds fixed. Its length does not.
harness.note.deferent-arm.ptolemaic.sate: The arm carrying {{bodyOf}} round its circle, drawn from the centre it is displaced about. It does not turn uniformly here: the point that makes it uniform is the equant, as far again beyond the centre.
harness.note.deferent-arm.copernican: The arm from the centre of the eccentric out to the centre of the epicyclet. It turns uniformly about the point it starts from, which is exactly what Copernicus wanted and the reason there is no equant in this model.
harness.note.deferent-arm.circle: The arm from {{centreOf}} to {{bodyOf}}. One arm at one uniform rate; there is nothing else in this model at all.
harness.note.epicycle-arm.ptolemaic: The arm from the epicycle's centre out to the planet. Compare its direction with the Sun's below: for an outer planet the two keep step, because this arm is the Earth's own orbit written into a geocentric model. Ptolemy could not have known it; Copernicus built a system out of noticing. The arm follows the mean Sun, so the two run a degree or two apart.
harness.note.epicycle-arm.copernican: The arm of the epicyclet, turning at twice the mean anomaly. It is a third of the centre's own displacement, and it is doing the last of the work the equant used to do.
harness.note.radius.kepler: The line from {{centreOf}} to the body — and the second law is its sweep. Run the clock and watch it move quickly near the nearest point of the orbit and slowly near the farthest, covering equal areas in equal times. Its rate against the mean rate below is that law as a number.
harness.note.radius.newton: The line the pull acts along. Everything the earlier models drew is scaffolding for describing a motion; this is the direction of the force, and the shape of the orbit follows from it.
harness.note.apsidal.ptolemaic: The axis the whole eccentric arrangement is built along: apogee at one end, perigee at the other, with the centre and the equant strung out between them. Ptolemy fixed it against the stars, and the app carries his value forward to J2000 by the true precession rather than by his own rate of one degree a century.
harness.note.apsidal.copernican: The line of apsides of the eccentric — the axis its displacement is measured along. Its two ends fall a little short of the orbit's own nearest and farthest points, because the epicyclet carries the rest.
harness.note.apsidal.kepler: The major axis, from the nearest point of the orbit to the farthest, through both foci. The entire eccentricity is the offset of {{centreOf}} along this line; the ellipse's own flattening is a fraction of a percent.
harness.note.velocity: The body's motion itself, drawn along its path. This is what no earlier model here contains: a state carried forward from one instant to the next, rather than a place read off a circle.
harness.note.net-force: Every pull on the body, added. This and the velocity are the whole of the model — where the body goes next follows from the two of them and from nothing else.
harness.note.gravity: How hard {{sourceOf}} pulls on {{bodyOf}}, along the line joining them, falling off as the square of the distance. The drawn lengths are ordered but deliberately not proportional — the Sun takes the overwhelming share, and at true proportion every other arrow would be invisible. These figures are exact.
harness.value.offsetRatio: As a fraction of the radius
harness.value.impliedDistance: Distance from the Sun this implies
view.scaleHint: Compressed scale shows every orbit at once; true scale keeps the distance ratios honest.
view.zodiac.label: Zodiac
view.constructionHint: Select a body to see its machinery — circles for Ptolemy and Copernicus, an ellipse for Kepler, force vectors for Newton.
view.constructionLegend: The thin circle is the deferent, the heavier one the epicycle. The open ring marks the deferent's centre; the diamond marks the equant, the point about which the epicycle's centre moves uniformly. The dashed line is the apsidal axis.
view.constructionScaleWarning: At compressed scale the curves appear distorted. Switch to true scale to see them in their true shape.
view.recentredSunJoint: Two motions, composed. The deferent is the orbit of {{origin}} run backwards, so what rides it is the Sun; {{epicycle}} then rides an epicycle about that Sun. Their sum is exactly where the model has already put the body — the overlay draws the composition and computes nothing of its own.
view.recentredEmptyJoint: Two motions, composed. The deferent is the orbit of {{deferent}}, drawn about the stationary point; the epicycle riding it is the orbit of {{origin}} run backwards. Nothing sits at the joint between them. Their sum is exactly where the model has already put the body — the overlay draws the composition and computes nothing of its own.
view.recentredSunOnly: Only one motion here, so nothing is composed: this is the orbit of {{origin}} run backwards, which is the Sun’s apparent path. The same curve is one of the two legs in every other body’s figure.
view.recentredNoOrbit: {{body}} goes round {{parent}} rather than the Sun, so its path is not one of the two this overlay composes — and the map draws that orbit enlarged besides, which a chain of true-scale legs could never meet. The composition is offered for the Sun and the planets.
view.recentredPtolemyInferior: Because the stationary body is the Earth, this is also Tycho’s arrangement, and it is how Ptolemy lays out an inferior planet: the Sun carries the epicycle.
view.recentredPtolemySuperior: Because the stationary body is the Earth, this is also how Ptolemy lays out a superior planet. His epicycle centre is an empty point too, and his epicycle arm stays parallel to the direction of the Sun — here that arm is the line from the Earth to the Sun, and the curve it sweeps is the Earth’s own orbit. That is where the Sun inside the model of every planet comes from.
sky.none: Select a body and this shows the patch of sky it is in, as seen from the observation point.
sky.caption: {{body}} among the stars, seen from {{observer}} · {{field}}° × {{height}}° of the ecliptic
sky.daylight: this part of the sky is above the horizon only by day
sky.flat: every body on the ecliptic: this construction has no latitude theory
sky.note: A chart of the zodiac band. Not a view through a window. Longitude runs to the right, latitude upward, both to the same scale — so a separation on screen is the separation in the sky. The app models no horizon and no time of day, so it does not pretend to know your left from your right.
sky.zoomNote: The wheel over the band widens or narrows the field, and a double-click puts it back to 40°. This is the band's own zoom: it has nothing to do with the map's magnification, which stays where you left it.
sky.starsNote: The stars are the brightest within 35° of the ecliptic, at their catalogued J2000 places — the landmarks every pre-telescopic position was measured against. Run the clock and watch the planet move against them, and turn back on itself.
export.failed: Couldn't save the image. Nothing else changed.
export.mapNote: Captures the map exactly as it stands — this model, this zoom, this date. SVG stays sharp at any size and opens as editable shapes; PNG is the one to paste into a slide.

locale.label: Language
info.forceScaleNote: Vector lengths are ordered but not proportional — the Sun is over 98% of the pull, so true proportions would leave the others invisible. Exact figures are in the table.
view.forcesLegend: The blue vector is velocity, the black one the net force. The thin vectors are each body's gravitational pull, coloured by which body pulls. Lengths are ordered, not proportional — exact figures are listed under the selected body.
view.sphere.frameHint: The celestial sphere is concentric with the map, as on a traditional orrery. Sight-lines bend at the body when the observer is not the centre.
view.sphere.observerHint: The celestial sphere surrounds the observation point — where the sky actually belongs. It is no longer concentric with the map, so the map shrinks to make room. Sight-lines still run observer → body → sphere. They pass through the body whatever the projection does.
theme.label: Look
view.zoomHint: The mouse wheel and the + / - keys zoom the map, dragging moves it, both about the stationary point. Double-click returns to the fitted view. On the realistic scale the zoom reaches far enough to separate the Moon from the Earth; bodies that fall off the map are then shown as pointers on its edge.
engine.help.ptolemaic-almagest: The same construction driven by Ptolemy's own mean motions and his precession — what a second-century astronomer would actually have computed. His rates are excellent, but the error is paid once per revolution: over nineteen centuries the outer planets drift about a degree, Venus and Mercury by tens.
events.comparison.referenceNote: Reference from the VSOP87 theory, times in UT. Within minutes of published values — under ten for both the 2020 Mars opposition and the great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn.
engine.help.vsop87: VSOP87, the analytical theory used here as the reference. Elliptical orbits with their mutual perturbations; the yardstick the three historical models are measured against.
engine.help.keplerian: Kepler's ellipses: the Sun at one focus, and a radius vector that sweeps equal areas in equal times. The same heliocentric arrangement Copernicus proposed, with the circles replaced — which is where the accuracy actually came from.
view.ellipseLegend: The curve is the orbit itself — an ellipse, not a circle. Both open rings are foci: the Sun sits on one, nothing at all on the other. The small ring between them is the geometric centre. It governs nothing now. The bright arm is the radius vector; run the clock and watch it sweep faster near the Sun.
view.osculatingLegend: The Moon is not placed by an ellipse — no fixed one fits it — so this is the two-body orbit its present position and speed imply, Earth at the focus. Run the clock and watch it breathe: the Sun's pull on the pair swings the eccentricity by a factor of three within months. That wandering is what Ptolemy chased with a crank and Newton finally explained.
calc.title: How the models were used
calc.intro: None of these models was a picture. Each was a procedure for turning a date into a number, and the numbers were the product. The Almagest is a book of tables. Kepler spent twenty-six years on the Rudolphine Tables.
calc.demonstrations.intro: The handful of moments when the models disagreed about something the sky could settle. Each sets the date, the model and the vantage.
calc.working.intro: Finding {{body}} on {{date}}, as each model required it to be done. Oldest first.
calc.working.moral: The labour climbs steeply from Ptolemy to Kepler, then stops. Ptolemy needs two table look-ups and two additions. Kepler needs a transcendental equation solved by iteration, per body and per date, by hand. Newton needs no new arithmetic at all — his two-body solution is Kepler's ellipse. What changed with him is that the ellipse stopped being fitted to observation and became a consequence of a force.
calc.selectBody: Select a body on the map to see each model's working for it.
calc.ptolemy.epicycleCentre: Mean longitude of the epicycle's centre
calc.cost.ptolemy: Two table look-ups and two additions. This is what an ephemeris cost for fourteen centuries.
calc.cost.ptolemySun: One table look-up and one addition — the Sun needed no equant.
calc.cost.copernicus: Two table look-ups and an addition. Much what Ptolemy cost. That is the awkward part of 1543: the new system was no cheaper to use and no more accurate, so its case had to rest on other grounds.
calc.cost.kepler: Newton–Raphson passes: {{iterations}} — because M = E − e sin E cannot be rearranged for E. Once per body, per date, by hand.
calc.cost.newton: No new arithmetic for one planet: the two-body problem solves in closed form to Kepler's own ellipse, so the column to the left is Newton's working too. What he added was the reason it holds — and a period that follows from the masses, which, run backwards, is how the Sun was weighed. Beyond two bodies there is no closed form; Newton attacked that by perturbation, and the {{evaluations}} force evaluations behind the last line are a modern stand-in he never had.
demo.venus-phases-1610.note: Kepler says three-quarters lit; Ptolemy says a crescent. With the spheres nested, Ptolemy cannot show more than half — so this is not a discrepancy but a contradiction, and it ended the geocentric system.
demo.mercury-transit-1631.note: Kepler predicted this transit in the Rudolphine Tables and did not live to see it; Gassendi watched it in Paris. Either it happens or it does not — the sharpest test a model can face.
demo.great-conjunction-1603.note: Jupiter and Saturn close at a few hundredths of a degree a day, so a small error in angle becomes an enormous one in time. The models fall days apart here.
demo.mars-opposition-1602: The Mars that broke the circle
demo.mars-opposition-1602.note: Mars is the most eccentric of the classical superior planets, so it is where circles fail worst. Kepler's eight arcminutes of leftover error came from oppositions like this one.
demo.great-conjunction-2020.note: The same crushing test, with a published time to check against: the reference lands within eight minutes of it.

bodies.label: Bodies
welcome.title: Four ways of predicting a planet
welcome.lede: The same sky, computed by Ptolemy, Copernicus, Kepler and Newton. Where they disagree is the interesting part.
welcome.point.models: Switch model in the top-left panel. Nothing else moves, so any change you see is the model's doing.
welcome.point.centre: Hold any body still — Earth for Ptolemy, the Sun for the rest — and watch every orbit redraw around it.
welcome.point.demos: Calculation & demonstrations opens the moments that settled the argument, and shows what each model cost to work by hand.
welcome.keys: Space plays and pauses, ← and → step a day, + and − zoom, Esc closes a panel. The ⓘ button in the top-right turns the explanatory text on and off.
calc.tables.ptolemy: The Almagest (c. AD 150) gives the tables and their derivation together; the Handy Tables were the working edition. Mean motions rested on Babylonian eclipse records centuries older — only a long baseline pins a rate down. So the whole scheme leaned on somebody else's observations. Each planet's eccentricity and epicycle had to be wrung geometrically out of a handful of chosen nights. The equation of argument changes with the epicycle's distance, which costs two tables and an interpolation between them. The Alfonsine Tables carried all this into Latin Europe. Three centuries later it was still in use, re-rooted whenever it drifted.
calc.tables.copernicus: De revolutionibus (1543) carried tables of its own. The ones people actually used were Reinhold's Prutenic Tables of 1551 — years of recomputation on Copernican parameters. They spread widely and were barely more accurate. The circles set the floor, and no care in the arithmetic could lift it. Copernicus had also thrown out the equant on principle and put small extra circles in its place, so what replaced Ptolemy's machinery was no simpler to tabulate.
calc.tables.kepler: The Rudolphine Tables, 1627 — twenty-six years after Tycho's observations reached him. A war ran through those years. So did a lawsuit with Tycho's heirs over the observations themselves, and his mother's trial for witchcraft. Every entry needed Kepler's equation solved by iteration. Halfway through he seized on Napier's logarithms and bound a table of them into the result. The work was finishable only because a new way of multiplying turned up while he did it. The Mercury transit of 1631 vindicated him. Older constructions put that transit on 4 November, when nobody would have been watching.
calc.tables.newton: The Principia (1687) contains no ephemeris at all. It is a book of theory, and closing the gap between the law and a usable table took another century of perturbation work. Clairaut's lunar theory gave the Moon's apsidal motion at half the observed rate. He came close to proposing an amendment to gravitation itself — then carried the approximation further, and it came right. Mayer's lunar tables of the 1750s won a share of the Longitude Prize. Tables in Newton's spirit came later still, from Laplace, Le Verrier and Newcomb.
engine.help.copernican: The heliocentric model as De revolutionibus actually describes it: each orbit an eccentric circle, with a small epicyclet replacing Ptolemy's equant. Copernicus split the eccentricity between the two, and the result follows an ellipse closely — his circles were never concentric.
info.ptolemyParts: Ptolemy gives no absolute distances. Every measurement in the Almagest is in parts of that body's own deferent, which he always takes as 60. Scale the whole construction up and the direction seen from Earth does not budge, so nothing he could observe would have fixed the real size. Each body's 60 is a different length. These figures do not compare between bodies.
bodies.focusHint: Click to select. Double-click to centre the map on it and zoom in.
track.title: Where {{body}} appears, night after night
track.none: Select a body to plot the track it traces against the stars.
track.hint: Longitude runs up the plot, time across it. This is the record an observer keeps: a body's place among the stars, night after night. Where the curve doubles back, the body is retrograde. The rings mark the two stations. Ptolemy's epicycle and Copernicus's moving Earth were both built to reproduce this one shape.
